# Dates and text {#sec-m1-datas-strings} In transport datasets, two kinds of column cause more work than all the others combined: **dates** (in inconsistent formats) and **text** (names of municipalities, facilities, commodities, addresses). This chapter handles both with `lubridate` and `stringr`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(lubridate) library(stringr) ``` ::: ## Dates with `lubridate` ### Reading `lubridate`'s functions are named after the order of the components: `lubridate::dmy()` for day-month-year, `lubridate::ymd()` for year-month-day, and so on. They tolerate different separators. Brazilian data usually come as day/month/year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lubridate::dmy("28/09/2026") #> [1] "2026-09-28" lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28") #> [1] "2026-09-28" lubridate::dmy(c("28/09/2026", "05-10-2026", "3 nov 2026")) #> [1] "2026-09-28" "2026-10-05" "2026-11-03" lubridate::ymd_hms("2026-09-28 14:00:00") #> [1] "2026-09-28 14:00:00 UTC" ``` ::: Note that `R` always **stores** a date in the `YYYY-MM-DD` format (it is the `Date` object, a number under the hood). The `28/09/2026` format only exists when **displaying** the date. To display or export in the Brazilian format, use `format()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28") format(d, "%d/%m/%Y") # "28/09/2026" #> [1] "28/09/2026" format(d, "%d de %B de %Y") # written out, in the system locale #> [1] "28 de September de 2026" ``` ::: The `%d/%m/%Y` pattern (day, month, 4-digit year) is the same vocabulary as `dmy()`/`ymd()`, only for formatting instead of reading: `%d` day, `%m` month, `%Y` 4-digit year, `%y` 2-digit year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lubridate::dmy("2026-09-28") # wrong order: returns NA with a warning #> [1] NA ``` ::: This is the most frequent error: reading a date column with the order swapped and getting `NA` in part of the rows. Always check: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} datas_texto <- c("28/09/2026", "30/09/2026", "31/02/2026", "") datas <- lubridate::dmy(datas_texto) datas #> [1] "2026-09-28" "2026-09-30" NA NA sum(is.na(datas)) # how many failed? #> [1] 2 datas_texto[is.na(datas)] # which ones? #> [1] "31/02/2026" "" ``` ::: ### Components and arithmetic ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28") lubridate::year(d); lubridate::month(d); lubridate::day(d) #> [1] 2026 #> [1] 9 #> [1] 28 lubridate::wday(d, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE) # depends on the system locale #> [1] Monday #> 7 Levels: Sunday < Monday < Tuesday < Wednesday < Thursday < ... < Saturday lubridate::quarter(d) #> [1] 3 lubridate::yday(d) # day of the year #> [1] 271 d + lubridate::days(15) #> [1] "2026-10-13" d + months(1) #> [1] "2026-10-28" d - lubridate::years(1) #> [1] "2025-09-28" lubridate::floor_date(d, "month") # first day of the month #> [1] "2026-09-01" lubridate::ceiling_date(d, "month") - lubridate::days(1) # last day of the month #> [1] "2026-09-30" ``` ::: ### Intervals and durations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} inicio <- lubridate::ymd("2026-09-28") fim <- lubridate::ymd("2026-11-05") fim - inicio # difftime, in days #> Time difference of 38 days as.numeric(fim - inicio, units = "days") #> [1] 38 lubridate::interval(inicio, fim) / months(1) # in months #> [1] 1.258065 lubridate::time_length(lubridate::interval(inicio, fim), "weeks") # in weeks #> [1] 5.428571 ``` ::: Typical application: trip duration from two timestamps (departure, `partida`, and arrival, `chegada`, of three ships). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} viagens <- data.frame( navio = c("Navio A", "Navio B", "Navio C"), partida = lubridate::ymd_hms(c("2026-03-01 08:30:00", "2026-03-02 22:10:00", "2026-03-04 06:00:00")), chegada = lubridate::ymd_hms(c("2026-03-04 17:45:00", "2026-03-07 09:05:00", "2026-03-05 23:30:00")) ) viagens$horas <- as.numeric(difftime(viagens$chegada, viagens$partida, units = "hours")) viagens$dia_semana <- lubridate::wday(viagens$partida, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE) viagens ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### Aggregating by period ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} viagens$mes <- lubridate::floor_date(viagens$partida, "month") aggregate(horas ~ mes, data = viagens, FUN = mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Time zone `lubridate::ymd_hms()` assumes UTC by default. For Brazilian GPS or GTFS data, give the time zone: `lubridate::ymd_hms(x, tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")`. Ignoring this produces three-hour errors in travel-time calculations. It is a recurring problem when comparing data from different sources. ::: ## Text with `stringr` All of the package's functions start with `str_`, take the text as their first argument and are vectorised. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cidades <- c(" Paranaguá ", "SÃO GONÇALO DO AMARANTE", "Rio Grande", "itajaí") stringr::str_trim(cidades) # removes spaces at the ends #> [1] "Paranaguá" "SÃO GONÇALO DO AMARANTE" #> [3] "Rio Grande" "itajaí" stringr::str_squish("Porto de Santos") # also removes repeated spaces #> [1] "Porto de Santos" stringr::str_to_upper(cidades) #> [1] " PARANAGUÁ " "SÃO GONÇALO DO AMARANTE" #> [3] "RIO GRANDE" "ITAJAÍ" stringr::str_to_lower(cidades) #> [1] " paranaguá " "são gonçalo do amarante" #> [3] "rio grande" "itajaí" stringr::str_to_title(stringr::str_to_lower(cidades)) #> [1] " Paranaguá " "São Gonçalo Do Amarante" #> [3] "Rio Grande" "Itajaí" stringr::str_length(cidades) #> [1] 12 23 10 6 ``` ::: ### Search, detect, replace ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} instalacoes <- c("Terminal Portuário do Pecém", "Porto de Santos", "IP4 Itacoatiara", "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil") stringr::str_detect(instalacoes, "Terminal") # TRUE/FALSE #> [1] TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE stringr::str_subset(instalacoes, "Port") # returns those that match #> [1] "Terminal Portuário do Pecém" "Porto de Santos" stringr::str_which(instalacoes, "Port") # positions #> [1] 1 2 stringr::str_replace(instalacoes, "Terminal", "Term.") # first occurrence #> [1] "Term. Portuário do Pecém" "Porto de Santos" #> [3] "IP4 Itacoatiara" "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil" stringr::str_replace_all(instalacoes, " ", "_") # all of them #> [1] "Terminal_Portuário_do_Pecém" "Porto_de_Santos" #> [3] "IP4_Itacoatiara" "Terminais_Fluviais_do_Brasil" stringr::str_remove_all(instalacoes, "^IP\\d+ ") # prefix such as "IP4 " #> [1] "Terminal Portuário do Pecém" "Porto de Santos" #> [3] "Itacoatiara" "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil" ``` ::: ### Extract and split ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sh2 <- c("CT-Contêineres", "27-Combustíveis", "10-Cereais") stringr::str_sub(sh2, 1, 2) # fixed position #> [1] "CT" "27" "10" stringr::str_split(sh2, "-", simplify = TRUE) # splits into a matrix #> [,1] [,2] #> [1,] "CT" "Contêineres" #> [2,] "27" "Combustíveis" #> [3,] "10" "Cereais" stringr::str_extract(sh2, "^[A-Z0-9]+") # before the hyphen #> [1] "CT" "27" "10" stringr::str_extract(sh2, "(?<=-).*$") # after the hyphen #> [1] "Contêineres" "Combustíveis" "Cereais" ``` ::: A very common case: splitting municipality and state from a single field. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} locais <- c("Paranaguá/PR", "Santos/SP", "São Luís/MA") data.frame( municipio = stringr::str_extract(locais, "^[^/]+"), uf = stringr::str_extract(locais, "[A-Z]{2}$") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### Regular expressions in a table | Pattern | Meaning | Example | |:--|:--|:--| | `^` / `$` | start / end of the text | `^BR` matches "BR-116" | | `\\d` | one digit | `BR-\\d{3}` matches "BR-116" | | `\\s` | space | `\\s+` one or more spaces | | `[A-Z]{2}` | two capital letters | state abbreviation | | `.` | any character | `a.c` matches "abc" | | `*` `+` `?` | 0+, 1+, 0 or 1 repetitions | `\\d+` a number | | `(?<=x)` | *lookbehind*: after "x" | `(?<=-)\\d+` | | `|` | or | `Porto|Terminal` | In R, the backslash must be doubled inside a string: `"\\d"` is the digit. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rodovias <- c("BR-116/PR", "BR 277", "PR-508", "br-153 km 45") stringr::str_extract(rodovias, "\\d{3}") #> [1] "116" "277" "508" "153" stringr::str_detect(stringr::str_to_upper(rodovias), "^BR") #> [1] TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE stringr::str_extract(rodovias, "(?i)km\\s*\\d+") #> [1] NA NA NA "km 45" ``` ::: ### Standardising to join datasets The most important use of `stringr` in the course: preparing a join **key**. Municipality names come with different accents, case and spacing in each dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} padronizar <- function(x) { x |> stringr::str_squish() |> stringr::str_to_lower() |> stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") |> # removes accents stringr::str_remove_all("[^a-z ]") # removes punctuation } base_a <- c("São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Paranaguá", " Rio Grande ") base_b <- c("SAO GONCALO DO AMARANTE", "PARANAGUA", "RIO GRANDE") data.frame( base_a, base_b, igual_cru = base_a == base_b, igual_pad = padronizar(base_a) == padronizar(base_b) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Standardising municipality names solves most cases, but **not all**: there are municipalities with the same name in different states (for example, *Bonito* exists in MS, PA, PE and BA). Whenever possible, use the **7-digit IBGE code** as the key, and the name only for human reading. We deal with this in @sec-m1-joins. ::: ### Building text ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} uf <- "PR"; tku <- 8.33 stringr::str_c("Ligação com destino ", uf, ": ", tku, " bi TKU") #> [1] "Ligação com destino PR: 8.33 bi TKU" stringr::str_glue("Ligação com destino {uf}: {tku} bi TKU") #> Ligação com destino PR: 8.33 bi TKU sprintf("Ligação com destino %s: %.2f bi TKU", uf, tku) #> [1] "Ligação com destino PR: 8.33 bi TKU" stringr::str_pad(c("1", "23", "456"), width = 3, pad = "0") # codes with leading zeros #> [1] "001" "023" "456" ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} We use `stringi::stri_trans_general()` instead of `iconv(to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")` because `iconv`'s result varies between Windows, macOS and Linux. On Windows, it sometimes returns `?` instead of the accented letter. `stringi` is already installed together with `stringr`. ::: `str_pad()` solves a classic problem: municipality or census tract codes read as numbers lose their leading zero. `str_pad(cod, 7, pad = "0")` restores them.
